newsitem.title: USA: McDonnell Douglas net hurt by costs, fewer launches.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell Douglas net hurt by costs, fewer launches.

text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corp., reporting lower first-quarter results, said Thurday its earnings were hurt by accident-related costs and fewer launches due to a Delta II rocket failure in January.
The aerospace giant also cited increased costs on its MD-95 commercial aircraft and Delta III development programmes, as well as costs related to its pending merger with Boeing Co.
McDonnell had first-quarter profits of $181 million, or 86 cents a share, on revenues of $3.23 billion. A year earlier it earned $198 million, or 89 cents a share, on revenues of $3.17 billion.
St. Louis-based McDonnell Douglas said its operating earnings in the military aircraft segment rose to $259 million in the first quarter from $250 million in the year-ago period.
Earnings in the F/A-18E/F military airplane programme increased, while results were lower from the F-15 and F/A-18C/D programmes, it added.
McDonnell said it has received approval from the Department of Defence to begin production of the first 12 aircraft in the F/A-18E/F programme.

The phase-in of work after a 99-day strike at its St. Louis operations, which ended in September 1996, along with increased retirements of experienced personnel late in the year, affected productivity, McDonnell added.
Military segment revenues in the first quarter were $1.9 billion, down from $2.0 billion in the 1996 quarter.

Revenues for missiles, space and electronic systems were $553 million, down from $608 million. Expenditures for the Delta III launch vehicle under development and lower earnings on the Delta II programme caused a decrease in results for this segment, McDonnell said.
Revenues for commercial aircraft were $624 million, up from $428 million a year ago.

Earnings from the sale of spare parts and related services contributed to earnings in the commercial aircraft segment. Increased losses on the MD-95 programme, currently in development, were partly offset by some reduction in cost estimates on prior deliveries of trijet and twin-jet aircraft.
McDonnell Douglas stock was off 37.5 cents at $59.50 in morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
